document.title: The Costs of Soviet Involvement in Afghanistan
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
document.note: Major CIA study examining all aspects of Russian involvement in Afghanistan and detailing costs, concluding they had grown steadily and would likely continue to rise but probably would not change Soviet larger purposes.

sources_cited: DI Intelligence Assessment NESA 85-10084 / SOV 85-10081 (1985): The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan: Five Years After
key_claims: The Soviets spent about 15 billion rubles on the conduct of the war from December 1979 through 1986, a modest share of defense spending.
Soviet troop strength rose gradually from about 80,000 in 1980 to about 120,000 in 1986, and the Soviets suffered an estimated 30,000-35,000 casualties, a third of whom died.
Rising costs are driven mainly by increased air operations and helicopter losses, with more than 300 aircraft lost in 1984-85, nearly 90 percent of them helicopters.
Soviet leaders privately concede that they miscalculated the difficulty and long-term costs of the war.
Economic cost is unlikely to force withdrawal; Moscow is willing to bear the burden rather than accept what would look like a defeat.
The Afghan army remains incapable of quelling the resistance, and the Soviet-installed Kabul regime remains weak.
The CIA estimates Soviet direct war costs from December 1979 through 1986 at about 15 billion rubles, or roughly $48 billion in 1984 US prices.
Afghan-related costs are only 2 to 2.5 percent of total Soviet defense spending and have risen about 12 percent a year.
Procurement, mainly ammunition and equipment replacement, was half of all costs; air munitions use rose sharply from 1983.
About 750 Soviet aircraft (high estimate) were destroyed through 1985, roughly 640 of them helicopters; the low estimate is 320.
The DRA pays for Soviet arms and part of economic aid, largely through natural gas sales.
The July 1986 withdrawal of six regiments was a sham, with fewer than 2,000 net troops withdrawn.
The CIA judged that the Soviets remained committed to a stable pro-Communist Kabul regime and that any decision to withdraw would rest on political and military rather than economic factors.
The Soviets do not appear ready to abandon their goal of a stable pro-Communist regime in Kabul that can rule without a large Soviet presence.
Recent changes in Soviet strategy, especially more air operations, raised costs somewhat faster than before, but the leadership sees the costs as relatively low.
The CIA assesses that any Soviet decision to withdraw would rest on political and military considerations rather than economic ones.
The Soviet propaganda campaign claiming a sincere search for a political solution is not matched by concessions affecting the military effort.
The CIA's use of full replacement costs put its procurement estimate on the high side; depreciated values would have lowered the 1980-86 total by 3-3.5 billion rubles.
The CIA assumed that no additional Soviet divisions were created because of the war, and treated ten new divisions as planned peacetime expansion.
